name: Skeleton watch

card.summary: A mechanical watch with a visible movement, worn as a statement accessory that adds technical, detailed character to an outfit.
card.price: Often thousands of dollars at the luxury end
card.note: Prices vary hugely across brands and movement types.

quick.overview:
A skeleton watch is a mechanical watch whose moving parts are visible through the front, back or a cutout in the dial. It is worn as a style accessory: the exposed gears give the wrist a distinctive, intricate look.

The form goes back to the 1760s, when French clockmaker André-Charles Caron is credited with creating it. Today the term covers fully skeletonised movements, semi-skeletons and open-heart dials.
quick.how: People wear it like any dress or statement watch, matching it to clothing and occasion. Lighter variants such as semi-skeleton or open-heart show only part of the movement.
quick.risks: No health risks. Luxury skeleton watches can be expensive, and the visible movement means the design is more delicate to produce than a standard dial.

lead: A skeleton watch is a mechanical watch in which the moving parts can be seen, through the front, through the back or through a small cutout in the dial [1]. 'True' skeletonisation trims metal from the bridges, plates and wheel train to leave a minimal framework, often engraved [1].

The design is attributed to the French clockmaker André-Charles Caron in the 1760s. Patek Philippe made skeleton pocket watches for display in the mid-1800s and began manufacturing them in the 1970s [1].

Variants include the semi-skeleton, with a partial dial cutaway, and the open-heart, with a round window onto the balance wheel [1]. Luxury versions cost thousands of dollars and some reach hundreds of thousands [1]. No clinical studies exist on the item.

chain: Wear a watch with a visible mechanical movement
Adds a detailed focal point at the wrist
Complements an outfit and signals interest in craft
angle.text: The watch is an accessory: its exposed movement adds a visual detail to the wrist that wearers use to finish a look. How it reads depends on the case, strap and the rest of the outfit.

infobox: Thousands of dollars and up at the luxury end

paras: Fully skeletonised watches remove non-essential metal from the movement; semi-skeleton designs cut away part of the dial; open-heart models show mainly the balance wheel, a style especially common on tourbillon watches [1].

Few skeleton watches were made in the 18th and 19th centuries because of the labour involved [1]. Patek Philippe produced display pieces in the mid-1800s and started regular production in the 1970s [1].

timeline.event: André-Charles Caron creates the skeleton watch [1].
Patek Philippe begins manufacturing skeleton watches [1].
